title: A hundred-year experiment in togetherness
text: The open-plan office {{1}} born in the 1950s, when German designers promoted a landscape style {{2}} desks drifted freely among plants rather than ranks. American firms, {{3}} liked the low cost as much as the modern look, spread the idea worldwide: costs could be cut {{4}} removing walls and doors, and floorspace per employee shrank year after year. But the research is unflattering. People in open offices suffer {{5}} interruptions, and they hold {{6}} face-to-face conversation than people behind walls, compensating with headphones and email. As a result, the pendulum {{7}} begun to swing back towards a blend of deep-focus rooms, small meeting booths and shared tables for those who genuinely want company. The office of the future, most designers now admit, needs {{8}} offer both silence and society.

gaps.hint: passive: the office ___ born in the 1950s
gaps.explanation: Past passive with a singular subject: was born.

gaps.hint: relative adverb: a style ___ desks drifted
gaps.explanation: 'Where' refers back to the style as the setting.

gaps.hint: relative: American firms, ___ liked the low cost
gaps.explanation: Non-defining relative after the comma referring to the firms.
'Suffer more interruptions' — an increase in countable interruptions.
Uncountable 'conversation' and a reduction: hold less.

gaps.hint: auxiliary: the pendulum ___ begun to swing
gaps.explanation: Present perfect with a singular subject: has begun.
